tip: Prices use 'it makes': Πόσο κάνει; (póso káni = how much does it make?) is the everyday 'how much is it?'
Prices 'make' in Greek: κάνει (kani) in Ο καφές κάνει τρία ευρώ is literally 'the coffee makes three euros'. That's normal shop talk – κοστίζει (kostizi = costs) sounds more formal.
No word for 'of' after amounts – the noun just follows: δύο κιλά ντομάτες (dhío kilá domátes = two kilos tomatoes).
The article works as 'per': οχτώ ευρώ το κιλό (okhtó evró to kiló = eight euros the kilo) – no extra word needed.
'Three' agrees: τρία (tría) with neuter nouns like τρία παιδιά (tría pedhiá = three children), τρεις (tris) with masculine and feminine.
With several items the price verb goes plural: Πόσο κάνουν δύο καφέδες; (póso kánun dhío kafédhes = how much are two coffees?)
Μισό (misó = half) agrees with its noun: μισό κιλό (misó kiló), but feminine μισή ώρα (misí óra = half an hour).
The ; ending Τι ώρα είναι; (Ti ora ine) is the Greek question mark – Greek asks with a semicolon, not the ? sign.
Even numbers carry gender: it's τρεις (tris) because the unspoken ώρες (ores = hours) is feminine. Counting euros, 'three' becomes τρία (tria).
'At' + clock time is στις (stis): στις εννιά (stis enniá = at nine). Hours count as a feminine plural, hence the plural 'at'.
Στις δύο (stis dhío = at two) uses a plural 'the' because clock times count feminine ώρες (ores = hours). Only one o'clock goes singular: στη μία (sti mia).
Parts of the day need no 'in' – just the article: το πρωί (to proí = in the morning), το βράδυ (to vrádhi = in the evening).
One o'clock is the odd one out: στη μία (sti mía), not στις (stis) – one is a single hour, so the 'at' word goes singular too.
Half past is 'and half': δώδεκα και μισή (dhódheka ke misí = twelve and half = 12:30).
Σε (se) + a time span means 'in': σε δεκαπέντε λεπτά (se dhekapénde leptá = in fifteen minutes).
Days are feminine – η Δευτέρα (i Dheftéra = Monday), η Τρίτη (i Tríti = Tuesday) – except neuter το Σάββατο (to Sávato).
No word for 'on' with days – the article alone does it: την Τετάρτη (tin Tetárti = on Wednesday).
No word for 'on' with days: το Σάββατο (to Sávato) is just 'the Saturday'. Every day works this way – only the article matches the day's gender: την Τρίτη (tin Tríti = on Tuesday).
No 'I' needed – the -ω ending of πίνω (pino) already marks the speaker. Greek drops subject pronouns unless you're stressing who does it.
Greek questions keep statement word order – no 'do'. Εσύ τρως κρέας; (esi tros kreas) = 'you eat meat?', asked by tone alone. That ; at the end is the Greek question mark.
Negation is usually just δεν (dhen) before the verb: δεν τρώω (dhen tró-o) = 'I don't eat'. No helper word like English 'do'.
Hunger is a verb, not a feeling you 'are': πεινάω πολύ (pináo polí = I hunger a lot) – no 'am' anywhere.
Thirst is a verb in Greek: διψάει (dhipsái) means 'is thirsty' – the baby thirsts. Hunger works the same way: πεινάει (pinái).
Talking about cheese in general still needs 'the': το τυρί (to tiri). Greek keeps the article where English drops it.
Ordering just names the item – no 'can I have' needed: Δύο καφέδες, παρακαλώ (dhío kafédhes parakaló).
'The bill' changes shape as an object: ο λογαριασμός (o loghariasmos) becomes τον λογαριασμό (ton loghariasmo). Articles and endings shift with the noun's role.
'One' matches its noun: ένα τσάι (ena tsai) but έναν καφέ (enan kafe) – masculine nouns as objects add -ν to the word for 'one'.
One word covers to, in, and at: σε (se). It fuses with 'the': σε + την becomes στην αγορά (stin aghorá) = to the market.
Πάμε (pame) is both 'we go' and 'let's go / shall we?' – the same form makes the statement and the invitation.
Στην (stin) loses its ν before most consonants: στη δουλειά (sti dhuliá = to work). It keeps the ν before vowels and hard sounds like k, p, t.
